questions.q: A bet: {p}% chance to win {w}, otherwise you lose {l}. What's the expected value per go, in £? (Use a minus sign if negative.)
Why does a casino win over time on roulette, even though players sometimes win big?
options: The green zero gives every bet a negative expected value for the player
Players always lose the first spin
Casinos only pay out on red
questions.why: On a European wheel, £10 on red has an EV of about −27p (−2.7%). Over thousands of spins that edge always wins.

questions.q: Match each activity to its usual expected value for an ordinary person.
pairs: Long-term investing in a global index fund
A fair coin flip with no fees
questions.why: Owning businesses has a positive expected return; casinos build in an edge; trading is roughly zero before costs and negative after.

questions.q: Making money trading for one month is good evidence that your approach has an edge.
questions.why: Short-run results are mostly luck. You need many trades, honestly tested, before results mean anything.

questions.q: What do UK CFD providers' required risk warnings typically show?
options: Most retail accounts lose money (around 68–82% at big providers)
About half win and half lose
questions.why: FCA rules make providers publish the share of retail accounts that lose money; at big UK providers it's typically around 68–82%.

questions.q: Which of these could be a genuine trading edge?
options: A tested strategy whose wins outweigh its losses after costs across many trades
A strong feeling that a share will rise
A share that has gone up three days in a row
A tip from a popular social media account
questions.why: An edge is a repeatable reason for positive expected value after costs. Feelings, recent moves and tips aren't edges.

questions.q: Put these in order of time horizon, shortest first.
items: Swing trading over a few weeks
Saving for a car in 3 years
questions.why: Day traders hold for minutes or hours, swing traders days or weeks, savers years, retirement investors decades.

questions.q: A strategy that loses 70% of the time must have a negative expected value.
questions.why: If the wins are big enough, EV can be positive: winning 30% at 4 times the loss gives 0.3 × 4 − 0.7 × 1 = +0.5.

questions.q: You win £{w} or lose £100 on each trade. What win rate (in %) makes the expected value exactly zero? (One decimal place.)
Explain why short-term trading usually has a negative expected value for beginners.

ideas.label: Before costs it's roughly zero-sum: one trader's gain is another's loss
Costs (spreads, fees, charges) push it below zero
Beginners are up against professionals with better tools and information

questions.model: Over short periods price moves are mostly noise and, before costs, one trader's gain is another's loss. Spreads, fees and overnight charges then push the average below zero. And beginners are up against professionals with faster systems and better information, so they have no edge.
questions.why: Zero-sum before costs, negative after, and the competition is strong.

tests.answer: It's zero sum before costs, the spread and fees make it negative, and you're against professionals with better information.
Because the app is rigged against you.

questions.q: Explain why judging a trade only by whether it made money can teach you the wrong lessons.

ideas.label: One result is mostly luck (a good decision can lose and a bad one can win)
Judge the process and expected value over many trades instead

questions.model: A single result is mostly luck: a good decision can lose and a bad one can win. If you judge by results, you might repeat reckless trades that happened to pay off. Judge the decision and process instead, and look at expected value over many trades.
questions.why: Decisions and results aren't the same thing.

tests.answer: One result is mostly luck, so you should judge the process and the expected value over many trades.
Because you might just have been lucky.
